title: Properties of water
blurb: Explain how water's polarity and hydrogen bonds produce cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling, floating ice and its power as a solvent.
question: On a hot afternoon a runner sweats heavily, yet her core temperature barely changes, and the electrolyte drink she sips dissolves instantly while a drop of oil from her snack floats on top. Which properties of water explain each of these observations?

teach.body: Formal definition: water (H2O) is a polar molecule. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, giving it a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge; the molecule is bent. Plain English: water is a tiny magnet with a negative end and a positive end. That lopsided charge is the reason for almost every special property of water that matters to life.

rows.label: Formed by
values: Partial + H attracted to partial - O

teach.body: Because each water molecule can hydrogen-bond to its neighbors, water sticks to itself (cohesion) and to other polar surfaces (adhesion). It takes a lot of heat to break those bonds, so water warms and cools slowly (high specific heat) and absorbs a lot of heat when it evaporates (high heat of vaporization). Freezing locks the bonds into an open lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats; liquid water is densest at about 4 °C.

teach.h: Properties of water and why they matter
head: Property
What it means
Example in life
rows: Surface tension; water pulled up xylem
Capillary action; meniscus in a tube
Ice floats and insulates a pond
teach.caption: Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level. It is the most abundant molecule in cells.
Capillary action needs both: adhesion pulls water up the surface and cohesion drags the rest of the water along.
"Universal solvent" is a nickname: water dissolves many substances, not all of them.
Water also ionizes slightly into H+ and OH-. In pure water the two are equal, so the pH is 7.

teach.body: Tanya, a nursing applicant, runs on a hot day. Her body is mostly water, and water's high specific heat means it absorbs a lot of heat with little temperature change, so her core stays near normal. Her sweat cools her because evaporating water absorbs a large amount of heat (high heat of vaporization). Her electrolyte drink dissolves because water's partial charges surround the ions, but the oil from her snack is nonpolar (hydrophobic), so it separates and floats.

teach.text: Exam reversals: OXYGEN is partially negative, hydrogen partially positive; hydrogen bonds are BETWEEN molecules (the bonds inside are polar covalent); cohesion is water to water, adhesion is water to something else; high specific heat means water RESISTS temperature change; ice is LESS dense than liquid water; evaporation COOLS; oils do not dissolve in water.

items: Water is polar: O partial negative, H partial positive, bent shape.
Hydrogen bonds link neighboring molecules; polar covalent bonds hold each molecule together.
Cohesion: surface tension. Adhesion: capillary action (with cohesion).
High specific heat stabilizes temperature; high heat of vaporization gives evaporative cooling.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
Water dissolves polar and ionic (hydrophilic) substances, not nonpolar (hydrophobic) ones.

summary: You can now explain why water is polar and how hydrogen bonds between molecules produce cohesion, adhesion, high specific heat, evaporative cooling and floating ice. You can also predict which substances dissolve in water and describe water's role in hydrolysis and dehydration synthesis.

A.q: Which bond holds the oxygen and hydrogen atoms together inside one water molecule?
A.why: Inside each water molecule, oxygen and hydrogen share electrons unequally: polar covalent bonds.

whyNot.0: Hydrogen bonds form BETWEEN neighboring water molecules, not inside one.
whyNot.2: Electrons are shared in water, not transferred, so the bonds are covalent, not ionic.
whyNot.3: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins.

A.q: Which property of water lets a column of water be pulled up through the narrow xylem of a tall tree?
A.why: Cohesion, from hydrogen bonds between water molecules, holds the water column together as it is pulled up the xylem.

whyNot.0: Specific heat is about resisting temperature change, not holding a column together.
whyNot.1: Ice density explains floating ice, not water movement in a plant.
whyNot.3: Hydrolysis uses water to break chemical bonds; it does not lift water.

A.q: Why does a lake freeze from the top down rather than from the bottom up?
options: Hydrogen bonds break as water freezes.
Ice is denser than liquid water.
Water at 0 °C is the densest water.
Ice is less dense than liquid water.
A.why: Freezing locks water into an open hydrogen-bonded lattice, so ice is less dense and floats, insulating the water below.

whyNot.0: Freezing forms stable hydrogen bonds; it does not break them.
whyNot.1: If ice were denser it would sink and lakes would freeze from the bottom.
whyNot.2: Liquid water is densest at about 4 °C, not at its freezing point.

B.q: Which property of water helps keep a person's body temperature stable when the surroundings warm or cool?
B.why: Water's high specific heat means it absorbs or releases a lot of heat with little change in its own temperature.

whyNot.1: Low specific heat would let body water heat and cool quickly, the reverse of what happens.
whyNot.2: Adhesion is water sticking to other surfaces; it does not hold heat.
whyNot.3: Ice density has nothing to do with body temperature.

B.q: Which part of a phospholipid molecule is hydrophobic?
B.why: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar, so they avoid water and point inward in a membrane.

whyNot.0: The phosphate head is polar and hydrophilic, facing the water.
whyNot.2: Charged groups attract water, so they are hydrophilic.
whyNot.3: Polar surfaces attract water; hydrophobic means nonpolar.

B.q: When water is used to break the bond between two monomers, what is the reaction called?
B.why: Hydrolysis ("water splitting") adds water to break a bond, as when digestion splits polymers into monomers.

whyNot.0: Dehydration synthesis releases water as it JOINS monomers.
whyNot.1: Condensation is another name for dehydration synthesis, which builds bonds.
whyNot.3: Ionization is water splitting into H+ and OH-, not the breaking of a bond between monomers.

C.q: Sweat evaporating from the skin cools the body. Which statement explains the cooling?
options: Evaporating water absorbs heat from the skin.
Water's high specific heat warms the skin.
Sweat releases its heat as it evaporates.
Adhesion traps body heat inside the sweat.
C.why: Water's high heat of vaporization means each gram that evaporates carries a large amount of heat away from the skin.

whyNot.1: Specific heat is resistance to temperature change; it does not warm or cool the skin by evaporation.
whyNot.2: Evaporation absorbs heat; releasing heat happens when vapor condenses.
whyNot.3: Adhesion keeps sweat on the skin but does not explain the cooling.

C.q: Which pairing of a property of water with its cause is correct?
options: Surface tension: adhesion of water to air
C.why: Capillary action happens as water adheres to a narrow tube's walls and cohesion pulls the rest of the column along.

whyNot.0: Surface tension comes from cohesion, water molecules pulling on each other.
whyNot.1: Ice floats because hydrogen bonds lock it into an open lattice; no covalent bonds break.
whyNot.2: Water dissolves salt because it is POLAR; its partial charges surround the ions.

C.q: Which description of the charges in a water molecule is accurate?
options: Oxygen partly positive; hydrogens partly negative
Oxygen partly negative; hydrogens partly positive
Both atoms neutral; electrons shared equally
Oxygen fully negative; hydrogens fully positive
C.why: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself, so it is partially negative and the hydrogens are partially positive.

whyNot.0: This reverses the charges; oxygen is the more electronegative atom.
whyNot.2: The sharing is unequal, which is why water is polar.
whyNot.3: Full charges come from transferring electrons (ionic bonds); water's charges are partial.

reteach.title: A crowd holding hands
reteach.question: Picture water molecules as a crowd of people who keep grabbing each other's hands. How does that picture explain water's properties?

blocks.body: Each person (water molecule) keeps grabbing the hands of neighbors (hydrogen bonds). A crowd holding hands is hard to break through: surface tension (cohesion). Some people also grab a railing: adhesion. To get the whole crowd moving faster you must pour in a lot of energy, because hands must keep letting go: high specific heat. Anyone who escapes the crowd takes a lot of energy with them: evaporative cooling. In winter they lock arms at full length and spread out: ice is less dense.

blocks.text: The hands are BETWEEN people: hydrogen bonds link different molecules, not the atoms inside one molecule.

explain.body: Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does. Oxygen becomes partially negative, the hydrogens partially positive, and the bent molecule has two charged ends.

test.q: Why is water described as a polar molecule?
options: It is held together by ionic bonds.
Its atoms carry full electric charges.
It mixes easily with oils and fats.
test.why: Unequal sharing of electrons gives oxygen a partial negative charge and the hydrogens partial positive charges.

whyNot.0: Water's bonds are polar covalent; electrons are shared, not transferred.
whyNot.1: The charges are partial, not full ionic charges.
whyNot.3: Water does NOT mix with nonpolar oils, because water is polar.

explain.body: The partially positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen of a neighbor. One hydrogen bond is weak, but billions together are strong.

test.q: In liquid water, hydrogen bonds form between:
options: The O and an H inside one molecule
The O of one molecule and an H of another
The two O atoms of neighboring molecules
The two H atoms inside a single molecule
test.why: A hydrogen bond links the partially positive H of one molecule to the partially negative O of a neighbor.

whyNot.0: O and H inside one molecule are joined by a polar covalent bond.
whyNot.2: Two oxygens are both partially negative and repel each other.
whyNot.3: The two hydrogens in one molecule are both partially positive and are not bonded to each other.

explain.body: Cohesion (water to water) gives surface tension. Adhesion (water to other polar surfaces) lets water climb fibers and tubes. High specific heat steadies temperature; high heat of vaporization makes sweating cool.

test.q: A paper towel soaks up a spill as water climbs its fibers. Which property is most responsible?
test.why: Water adheres to the polar cellulose fibers and, with cohesion, is drawn up through them (capillary action).

whyNot.0: Specific heat concerns temperature change, not movement up fibers.
whyNot.1: Heat of vaporization concerns evaporation, not soaking up a spill.
whyNot.3: Ice density has no role in a paper towel soaking up liquid water.

explain.body: Water's partial charges surround ions and polar molecules and pull them apart, so salts and sugars dissolve (hydrophilic). Nonpolar oils cannot hydrogen-bond with water and separate out (hydrophobic).

test.q: Why does table salt dissolve readily in water?
options: Water's partial charges attract its ions.
Salt is a nonpolar compound, like water.
Water is nonpolar and surrounds the salt.
Hydrogen bonds inside the salt break up.
test.why: The partially negative oxygens surround Na+ and the partially positive hydrogens surround Cl-, pulling the ions apart.

whyNot.1: Salt is ionic and water is polar; neither is nonpolar.
whyNot.2: Water is polar; that is what lets it dissolve ionic salt.
whyNot.3: Salt is held by ionic bonds, not hydrogen bonds.
